summary: Defines requirements for EAP methods used in IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs, which use 802.1X and EAP under the IEEE 802.11i security amendment. The material was approved by IEEE.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4017 lists the security features an EAP authentication method needs for IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs. A method must derive strong keys and protect the exchange against several attacks to meet the mandatory requirements.

what is the eap msk and emsk
subtitle: The required, recommended and optional features for EAP methods used in wireless LANs.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.11i uses EAP for authentication and key exchange, but EAP methods differ in the security properties they provide.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists mandatory, recommended and optional capabilities for EAP methods in IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs, including key derivation, mutual authentication and replay protection.
tldr.outcome: Methods that fail a MUST requirement are non-compliant with these requirements. RFC 4017 is Informational and presents material approved by IEEE 802.11.

today: RFC 4017 is an Informational memo published in March 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Wireless LANs Need EAP Requirements
sections.content:
IEEE 802.11i uses IEEE 802.1X, which relies on the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP). Wireless LAN deployments can use methods based on certificates, user names and passwords, secure tokens or mobile-network secrets.

This document sets requirements for EAP methods used in IEEE 802.11 deployments. The material was approved by IEEE 802.11 and is published as an Informational RFC. A method claiming conformance must complete IETF Last Call review.
sections.plainLanguage: Wireless LANs can use different EAP methods to check a user's identity. This memo lists the security capabilities those methods need for IEEE 802.11 use.

sections.title: Participants and Compliance Levels
sections.content:
The authenticator starts EAP authentication, and the peer responds. IEEE 802.1X calls the peer the supplicant. An EAP server terminates the method with the peer; it may run on a backend authentication server.

A method is not compliant if it fails any MUST or MUST NOT requirement. A method that meets every MUST and MUST NOT but misses a SHOULD or SHOULD NOT is conditionally compliant. A method that meets both the mandatory and recommended requirements is unconditionally compliant.
sections.plainLanguage: The authenticator starts the exchange and the peer responds. Passing every mandatory requirement gives conditional compliance; meeting the recommended requirements as well gives unconditional compliance.

sections.title: Mandatory Security Requirements
sections.content:
A suitable EAP method MUST derive symmetric keying material with 128 bits of effective strength. It must export a Master Session Key (MSK) and an Extended Master Session Key (EMSK), each at least 64 octets long. The method must support mutual authentication and leave the peer and server with equivalent method state.

The method must resist dictionary attacks and protect against man-in-the-middle attacks, including through cryptographic binding, integrity protection, replay protection and session independence. If it negotiates a ciphersuite, it MUST protect that negotiation. The EMSK is not shared with the authenticator or another third party.
sections.plainLanguage: An EAP method must create strong keys, authenticate both sides and protect the exchange from replay and interception. It must also protect any negotiated choice of cryptographic algorithms.

sections.title: Recommended and Optional Features
sections.content:
EAP methods SHOULD support fragmentation and reassembly when their payloads can exceed the minimum EAP MTU of 1020 octets. They SHOULD also support hiding the end user's identity.

Channel binding and fast reconnect are optional features; a method MAY support them. The memo distinguishes these recommendations and options from mandatory compliance requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Fragmentation and hiding the user's identity are recommended features. Channel binding and fast reconnect are optional, not mandatory.

sections.title: Methods That Do Not Meet the Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC identifies EAP-MD5-Challenge, One-Time Password and Generic Token Card as non-compliant with these wireless LAN requirements. It says these methods do not support any of the mandatory requirements, including key derivation and mutual authentication.

The RFC's conclusion concerns compliance with this document's criteria. It does not define a replacement authentication method.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists EAP-MD5-Challenge, One-Time Password and Generic Token Card as failing its mandatory criteria. These examples lack required features such as key derivation and mutual authentication.

sections.title: Security Threats Addressed by the Criteria
sections.content:
Because a wireless signal can be reached by an attacker within range, the memo connects its requirements to threats described in RFC 3748. Key strength addresses strong session keys; mutual authentication verifies both participants; and replay protection helps prevent reuse of old exchanges.

Protected ciphersuite negotiation helps prevent an attacker from changing the algorithm selection. Identity hiding is recommended, and channel binding is optional. Authorization is handled through other means, such as AAA protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements address specific risks, including replay, impersonation and altered algorithm choices. Authorization is a separate function and may use an AAA protocol.

viz.caption: Mandatory properties an EAP method must support

items.title: Key derivation
items.text: Generate symmetric keying material with the required strength.

items.title: Mutual authentication
items.text: Support authentication of both the peer and server.

items.title: Replay and interception protection
items.text: Protect against man-in-the-middle attacks, including replay.

items.title: Protected negotiation
items.text: Protect ciphersuite negotiation if the method negotiates one.
